question: What questions does Habakkuk ask God right at the beginning, and what does he see around him?
The word חָמָס (chamas, “violence”) appears in the prophet's cry and then with the Chaldeans: what changes when the violence comes from outside?
What is Habakkuk's second complaint, and why does God's answer about the Chaldeans leave him even more perplexed?
“How long, O LORD?”: do you feel free to ask God honest questions, as Habakkuk does?
What does the prophet do after his complaint, and what instructions does he receive about the vision?
The word אֱמוּנָה (emunah, “faith, faithfulness”) is at the center of verse 4: what difference does it make to read “faith” or “faithfulness,” and how does Paul take up this phrase in Romans 1:17?
The five “woes” denounce different sins of the oppressor: what are they, and what fate is repeated in each one?
“Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come”: what helps you wait when a promise is slow to be fulfilled?
What contrast does the chapter draw between mute idols and the LORD in His holy temple, before whom the earth is silent?
What does Habakkuk ask of God at the beginning of the prayer, and what word does he use when he recalls wrath?
What memories of Israel's history, such as the exodus and the ancient wars, does the prayer seem to evoke in its images of sea, rivers and mountains?
The verb עָלַז (alaz, “rejoice, exult”) appears in a context of losses: what kind of joy does verse 18 describe?
If the fig tree does not blossom in your life, in what will you still be able to rejoice?
